item.title: DeepSeek limits free chat: users complain about quotas
item.description:
DeepSeek users report new restrictions in the web version and app. After exhausting the daily quota, the service suggests waiting, and long dialogues and messages are now additionally limited. The most likely reason is a shortage of computing power. Against this backdrop, rumors have emerged about a possible paid subscription. Mentions of a quota system and the Coding Plan tariff were found in the web version's code. There is no official announcement of the subscription, its cost, or launch dates yet. Currently, DeepSeek earns primarily from its API, while the user chat remains free. Read more

item.title: Qwen4-Max is Out. What's the Difference from the Preview Version?
item.description:
On November 16, just five days after the preview version was shown, Alibaba released the full flagship model Qwen4-Max. This is a multimodal MoE giant with 2.4 trillion parameters (71 billion active) and a context window of 1 million tokens, optimized for complex coding, agent mode operation, and project prototyping – from frontend to 3D games. The model is focused on programming, solving complex multi-level tasks, and creating projects, including games. The model weights are currently closed, and it cannot be deployed on your own computer. Access is only available through the cloud and API (although developers promise to release more compact versions of the Qwen4 lineup in open source later). Below, we analyze the release architecture and look at the benchmarks. Read more

item.title: AI Trainer for Court Proceedings ChatCourt
item.description:
Hello, Habr! Imagine a typical university assignment. The instructor asks a neural network to create a task, the student gives it to their neural network and submits the finished answer, and a neural network checks the work again. From task preparation to checking, it turns into a correspondence between the student's AI and the instructor's AI — the irony is that it could be the same model. And people in such correspondence only pass texts to each other and act as living proxies. Of course, this doesn't always happen, and not all instructors create assignments using neural networks, and not all students solve homework with their help. But this scenario can no longer be called a rarity. At the same time, banning chatbots is pointless — they are already part of our daily lives, like the internet and smartphones. Read more

item.title: And So It Will Be Understood: How to Shorten Prompts and Calculate Losses
item.description:
The more detailed the prompt, the better the answer, and now context, role, constraints, and a couple of extra explanations are added to the task just in case. Half a page in, and it's already scary to delete anything, what if the whole thing rests on this very phrase. We looked at what research says about this. Spoiler: the prompt can be reduced many times over without a noticeable loss in answer quality. I'm trying to figure out which details the model can handle, and without which it will start to fantasize. Read more

item.title: Harness² — A New Generation of AI Agents from Google Research
item.description:
AI agents are rapidly evolving. Not long ago, an AI agent was just a chat with an LLM, doing whatever it pleased. But recently, you might have heard terms like skills, MCP, orchestration loop, tools, context management – all components of an agent system called Harness. The agent itself is LLM + Harness. With skillful use, even a less capable model with a quality Harness environment can outperform a top LLM without such an integration. There's a lot of talk about Harness itself lately. Skills, MCP, tools, orchestration, and sub-agents are all recent innovations. However, the current state has shortcomings: in one configuration, an agent reads directory structures, finds key files, and requests specific snippets. In another, it greedily reads everything, filling up the context. Or an agent might forget something, or misuse tools and MCP/sub-agent calls. Engineers then tweak Harness settings. But manual tuning is difficult and resource-intensive. Now, Google has released the open-source framework Harness² for self-improving AI agents. It allows agents in OpenCode and Codex to independently adjust instructions, skills, and other components during operation. This article explores Harness² – a plug-and-play framework from Google Research for recursive harnessing in an open world. Read on

item.title: How we fought with stress in Russian TTS: a pre-synthesis gate, text substitutions, and open questions
item.description:
I'm making "Channel 15" - a companion radio for Euro Truck Simulator 2: eighteen fictional truckers chat on the player's airwaves, respond to voice, and remember it between trips. We have three engines for voice acting: ElevenLabs (eleven_v3), OpenAI-compatible gpt-audio via OpenRouter, and a local clone on XTTS. The text pool is about four thousand lines, and it quickly became clear that all three engines, in different ways, confidently place Russian stress incorrectly. The night greeting "gudni" was read as "gUdni" - like a command, "yogurts", "kOzel" instead of, well, you know, nicknames and call signs like "mikhalych" and "bibi, kni" broke in their own ways. Here's what I built, where I hit a wall, and what remains an open question. Read more

item.title: Independent as Concepts, Dependent as Operations: Sampling Parameters in LLM Inference
item.description:
LLM inference infrastructure is traditionally optimized for throughput and latency: KV cache, CUDA graphs, batching, quantization, parallelism. These components form the "skeleton" of the system and define its performance limits. However, often overlooked is the layer that determines quality rather than speed: sampling parameters. These are the rules for selecting the next token from the logit distribution at each decoding step. Read more

item.title: Why 94% of AI Answers Ignore Company Websites
item.description:
Businesses today face a peculiar problem: their websites rank well in search results, but when clients ask AI assistants like ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google's AI Overviews for contractors, the companies themselves are absent from the answers. Instead, AI aggregates information from external directories and reference sites. To understand how AI models select candidates, I ran two hundred real B2B queries and traced the search process. In 94 out of 100 industry-specific selections, AI Overviews were generated, but corporate websites were rarely included. I then compared these results with monthly crawler statistics from an open organization directory, where each listing is available in HTML, Markdown, and JSON. This revealed why even a `llms.txt` file in the website's root is ineffective and what needs to be done to ensure businesses are included in recommendations. Read on.
